title: Florence Nightingale
wiki_lead:
Florence Nightingale ()  (12 May 1820 – 13 August 1910) was an English social reformer, statistician and the founder of modern nursing. Nightingale came to prominence while serving as a manager and trainer of nurses during the Crimean War, in which she organised care for wounded soldiers at Constantinople. She significantly reduced death rates by improving hygiene and living standards. Nightingale gave nursing a favourable reputation and became an icon of Victorian culture, especially in the persona of "The Lady with the Lamp" making ward rounds for wounded soldiers at night.
Recent commentators have asserted that Nightingale's Crimean War achievements were exaggerated by the media at the time, but critics agree on the importance of her later work in professionalising nursing roles for women. In 1860, she laid the foundation of professional nursing with the establishment of her nursing school at St Thomas' Hospital in London. It was the first secular nursing school in the world and is now part of King's College London. In recognition of her pioneering work in nursing, the Nightingale Pledge taken by new nurses, and the Florence Nightingale Medal, the highest international distinction a nurse can achieve, were named in her honour, and the annual International Nurses Day is celebrated on her birthday. Her social reforms included improving healthcare for all sections of British society, advocating better hunger relief in India, helping to abolish prostitution laws that were harsh for women, and expanding the acceptable forms of female participation in the workforce.
Nightingale was an innovator in statistics; she represented her analysis in graphical forms to ease drawing conclusions and actionables from data. She is famous for usage of the polar area diagram, also called the Nightingale rose diagram, which is equivalent to a modern circular histogram or pie chart. This diagram is still regularly used in data visualisation.
Nightingale was a prodigious and versatile writer. In her lifetime, much of her published work was concerned with spreading medical knowledge. Some of her tracts were written in simple English so that they could easily be understood by those with poor literary skills. Much of her writing, including her extensive work on religion and mysticism, has only been published posthumously.

Early life

Florence Nightingale was born on 12 May 1820 at Villa Colombaia, near the Porta Romana in Florence, where her parents, William Edward Nightingale and Frances "Fanny" (née  Smith), were staying during a European tour. Like her older sister Frances Parthenope, who had been named partly after Parthenope, the Greek settlement on the site of Naples, Nightingale was named after her birthplace. The family returned to England in 1821, when Nightingale was a year old. Lea Hurst in Derbyshire became one of her early homes, though the family first lived at Kynsham Court, Presteigne, while Lea Hurst was being completed. From 1825, after William Nightingale purchased Embley Park in Hampshire, the family divided its time chiefly between Embley and Lea Hurst, with some time also spent in London.
William Edward Nightingale had been born William Edward Shore, and assumed the Nightingale name after inheriting the Lea estate from Peter Nightingale. Fanny Nightingale was the daughter of the abolitionist and Unitarian William Smith. 
William Nightingale held views on women's intellectual education that were advanced for his time. Although the daughters had a governess in their early years, William supervised their education and provided much of their later instruction himself. Their curriculum included French, German, Italian, Latin, Greek, mathematics, constitutional history, grammar, composition, English literature and music. Nightingale's study of Latin had practical value in later life, as it sometimes enabled communication with abbots and monks she encountered while travelling. 
In 1838, William Nightingale took the family on another European tour, during which Nightingale met the English-born Parisian hostess Mary Clarke. Clarke became close to the Nightingale family, especially Florence, whom she treated as an intellectual equal. Clarke disliked the social conventions that constrained upper-class young women, reportedly saying that, if forced to choose, she would rather be "a galley-slave" than a woman. Her independence and intellectual circle helped show Nightingale a world in which women could participate in intellectual life alongside men.


Nursing vocation and training
On 7 February 1837, at the age of sixteen, she experienced what she later described as the first of several calls from God to service, though the call did not specify what form that service should take. It took several years for her vocation to become focused on nursing, and resistance from her mother and sister, Parthenope, delayed her attempts to act on it. Despite the anger and distress of her mother and sister, she rejected the expected role for a woman of her status to become a wife and mother. Nightingale worked hard to educate herself in the art and science of nursing, in the face of opposition from her family and the restrictive social code for affluent young English women.
As a young woman, Nightingale was described as attractive, slender, and graceful. While her demeanour was often severe, she was said to be very charming and to possess a radiant smile. Her most persistent suitor was the politician and poet Richard Monckton Milnes, but after a nine-year courtship, she rejected him, convinced that marriage would interfere with her ability to follow her calling to nursing.
In Rome in 1847, she met Sidney Herbert, a politician who had been Secretary at War (1845–1846) who was on his honeymoon. He and Nightingale became lifelong close friends. grok_lead: Florence Nightingale (12 May 1820 â 13 August 1910) was an English social reformer, statistician, and nurse regarded as the founder of modern nursing for her systematic reforms in hospital sanitation, nurse training, and public health data analysis. Born to a wealthy British family in Florence, Italy, she rejected a conventional life of leisure to pursue vocation in caregiving, training in Germany and Paris before leading 38 nurses to the Crimean War front in 1854, where British military hospitals at Scutari faced catastrophic mortality from disease exceeding battle wounds. There, Nightingale implemented empirical interventions targeting filth, poor ventilation, and inadequate nutritionâflushing sewers, laundering linens, procuring fresh food, and enforcing hygiene protocolsâwhich reduced hospital death rates from over 40% to under 2% by war's end, validating sanitation as the primary causal factor in preventable mortality over prevailing theories of miasma or contagion. Her statistical innovations, including polar area diagrams in her 1858 confidential report to Parliament, graphically demonstrated how administrative neglect caused excess deaths, influencing the Royal Commission on army health and broader sanitary reforms. Post-war, Nightingale established the Nightingale Training School at St Thomas' Hospital in 1860, standardizing nurse education with emphasis on observation, discipline, and evidence-based practice, while authoring Notes on Nursing (1859) to codify principles of patient care grounded in environmental control rather than medical intervention alone. Though romanticized as the "Lady with the Lamp" for nocturnal patient visits, her legacy rests on causal insights into hygiene 's role in survival, derived from rigorous data collection amid institutional resistance, establishing nursing as a data-informed profession independent of physician oversight.
